summary.text: The Big Bang is a physical theory describing how the universe expanded from an early state of high density and temperature.
Its models explain the abundance of light elements, the cosmic microwave background, the redshift of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the universe.
Measurements of the expansion place the age of the universe at an estimated 13.787 billion years, and a wide range of evidence strongly favors the model.

facts.label: Microwave glow
facts.value: The CMB was accidentally discovered in 1964

facts.label: Today's contents
facts.value: Dark matter makes up 27% and dark energy 68%

items.prompt: In the 1960s radio astronomers found a glow that looked the same in every direction. Why did that count against the steady-state rival?

options.label: It showed galaxies were all moving toward us
It proved the universe has no age at all
It matched stars simply being born and dying forever
Its uniformity and energy curve fit a hot, dense distant past

items.explain: The radiation's uniformity and the shape of its energy curve both fit Big Bang models of high temperature and density, and by the late 1960s most cosmologists dropped the steady-state model.

items.prompt: Looking in opposite directions, the universe appears remarkably alike. Which idea within Big Bang models accounts for that?

options.label: A phase of accelerated expansion in the earliest stages
Dark energy speeding up the expansion in recent times
Gravity pulling matter together into galaxies
Dark matter holding galaxies together as they spin

items.explain: The observed uniformity is explained through cosmic inflation, a phase of accelerated expansion during the earliest stages.

items.prompt: The first stars and galaxies formed from leftovers of the young universe. What were those leftovers mostly?

options.label: Mostly carbon, with some iron and oxygen
Mostly helium, with some hydrogen and gold
Mostly hydrogen, with some helium and lithium
Equal shares of hydrogen, silicon and iron

items.explain: The primordial elements were mostly hydrogen, with some helium and lithium, and they coalesced under gravity aided by dark matter.

items.prompt: Astronomers measure the redshifts of distant exploding stars and find the expansion is speeding up. What is that attributed to?

options.label: The extra matter left by baryon asymmetry
A concept called dark energy
A reheating event after inflation ended
The pull of dark matter around galaxies

items.explain: Redshifts of supernovae indicate accelerating expansion, an observation attributed to dark energy.

items.prompt: The universe has a finite age and light has a finite speed. What does that mean for the most distant things we can see?

options.label: Every event in the past has already sent its light to Earth
Light slows down once it has crossed a certain distance
Distant objects stop emitting light after a certain age
Light from some past events has not yet had time to reach Earth

items.explain: Since the universe has a finite age, there may be past events whose light has not reached Earth, which sets a past horizon on the most distant observable objects.

items.prompt: Which puzzle do Big Bang models still leave inadequately explained?

options.label: Why matter is more abundant than antimatter
Why the microwave background looks the same everywhere
Why galaxies appear to be moving away from us
Why the early universe was mostly hydrogen

items.explain: The unequal abundances of matter and antimatter, called baryon asymmetry, remain unexplained, while the microwave background, redshift and element abundances are explained.
